newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Peters signals tougher debt repayment stance.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Peters signals tougher debt repayment stance.

text.p: Treasurer Winston Peters on Tuesday signalled a tougher stance on long term debt repayment by shifting the government's long term fiscal aims from balance over the economic cycle to surpluses over the economic cycle.

In its Budget Policy Statement (BPS) the centre-right National-New Zealand First coalition government said it was aiming to reduce gross government debt below 30 percent of gross domestic product and net debt below 20 percent of GDP and then further lower gross and net debt consistent with running surpluses, on average, over the cycle.

The previous conservative National government's position was to reduce net debt to prudent levels, defined as less than 20 percent of GDP, and then lower debt below that level while maintaining at least fiscal balance over the cycle.
Peters also signalled his personal preference for further big reductions in public debt.
Talking to journalists at the release of the BPS, Peters said the government was carrying a prudent level of debt, but he did not want to speculate on how it would demonstrate a prudent debt level.
"My personal view is that if you have got the debt you should repay it unless for some interest rate condition it is wise not temporarily to do that.

"If you are paying higher than necessary interest rates because of the debt problem then I think long term, maybe ten or twenty years down the track, another government would find my view that nil debt and a credit circumstance is a wise position to be in," Peters said.
"I have difficulty understanding why paying back so much debt is wise and then stopping is also wise."
Peters' fiscal plan was attacked by the opposition Labour Party's finance spokesman Michael Cullen.
"The latest target is net public debt of 17.8 percent of GDP by the 1999/2000 year.

"That is well within the bounds of prudence in anyone's book -- what we need to see now is how the government plans to move from amassing ongoing surpluses to a balanced budget over the economic cycle," Cullen said.
While tightening its long term fiscal plans the coalition government loosened its short term plans.

The centre-right coalition between the conservative National Party and nationalist New Zealand First, formed after a general election in October, agreed to $5 billion of extra spending over three years.
It plans to spend an extra NZ$0.95 billion in the 1997/98 year, $1.7 billion more in 1998/99 and $2.35 billion in election year, 1999/2000.
The Budget itself will be in June but the BPS outlines the government's long term fiscal plans, its debt targets and taxation intentions.
